task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of August 17, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style newspaper explainer answering why readers can wait for a library e-book even though a digital file does not wear out or sit on a physical shelf.

facts.text: In August 2026, Talver Library lists 27 waiting accounts for the original fictional novel A Map of Last Ferries by Oren Vale.
The library holds three active digital licenses for the novel, each permitting one borrower at a time.
The normal digital loan lasts 14 days, although borrowers may return it early and unclaimed reservations can expire.
The 27-account queue therefore does not establish one exact waiting time for every reader.
Each license cost $72 and expires after 24 loans or two years, whichever comes first, under this title's contract.
The initial purchase of three licenses cost $216 and permits at most 72 completed loans before loan-count limits require replacement licenses.
The current licenses have been used for 21, 20 and 20 loans, respectively, leaving three, four and four loan uses under their count limits.
Buying a replacement license restores an expiring permission; it is not automatically an additional simultaneous lending slot.
Buying another concurrently active license would increase simultaneous capacity but would require additional budget.
A print copy of the same novel costs the library $18 before its own processing expenses and can circulate until it needs replacement.
A print copy is not available remotely in the way an e-book is, and transport to a branch is a barrier for some readers.
Reader Neri Moss uses enlarged digital text and says a print copy is not an equivalent substitute for her reading needs.
Moss said, "The file can reach my house instantly. The permission to borrow it is what I am waiting for."
Librarian Iva Drel says popular titles can consume budget through both additional capacity and license renewal.
Drel said, "Renewing what we already had and adding another copy are two different purchases."
The publisher says licensing receipts support rights payments and distribution; it has not supplied title-level costs or margins.
Other publishers and titles offer different license models, so these limits are not universal e-book rules.
The library's annual digital-material budget is $42,000 and also pays for databases and other titles.
Talver began lending e-books in 2011 and retains a home-delivery service for some physical materials.
The record contains no proposal to charge an extra per-loan fee to individual e-book borrowers.

forbidden_additions: An exact wait for every reader, unlimited simultaneous copying or one universal publisher model
Replacement licenses always add capacity or borrowers face a newly adopted per-loan fee
